There is an old problem in digital marketing: complex topics are far too easily packaged into one alarming but convenient formula. On the German web, this is often visible in discussions around the GDPR: instead of analyzing the site configuration, the owner is told that the absence of a cookie banner already makes the site vulnerable. For practical work, that is a poor starting point.

- If you look at a website as a system, the question starts with facts. Which marketing and third-party elements are actually present: analytics, GTM, pixel, video embeds, maps, reCAPTCHA, forms, chat, booking? What loads before consent, and what is blocked? Without this, it is impossible to determine honestly whether a CMP is needed or whether the problem has been framed incorrectly from the outset.
- For the marketer, there is also a disciplinary lesson here. Any tag or widget is not just a "tool," but a dependency with legal, analytical, and UX implications. When these dependencies are not documented, the team loses control: data is collected in unclear ways, the site changes in fragments, and the client receives outside interpretations that then have to be dealt with after the fact.
- I think it is useful to distinguish between two types of communication. The first explains conditions: if X is present, Y is required. The second creates universal anxiety. The first builds trust and working processes. The second creates noise and a short-term commercial impulse. For the industry, that is a fundamental difference.

How do you document consent-relevant tools on projects so that marketing, development, and the site owner all see the same picture?

---
